items.stem: Define the term "corpus luteum".
items.answer: The structure formed from the follicle after ovulation, which secretes progesterone
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the structure formed from the follicle after ovulation, which secretes progesterone. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "Progesterone triggers ovulation." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The LH surge triggers ovulation; progesterone is secreted afterwards by the corpus luteum.
items.markingKey: The LH surge triggers ovulation; progesterone is secreted afterwards by the corpus luteum. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why are women given hormones before IVF?
options: To suppress the natural cycle and then stimulate many follicles to develop so several eggs can be collected.
items.answer: To suppress the natural cycle and then stimulate many follicles to develop so several eggs can be collected.
items.markingKey: D. Superovulation.

A contraceptive pill contains synthetic oestrogen and progesterone. How does it prevent ovulation?
options: It inhibits FSH and LH secretion by negative feedback, so follicles do not mature and no LH surge occurs.
items.answer: It inhibits FSH and LH secretion by negative feedback, so follicles do not mature and no LH surge occurs.
items.markingKey: A. Negative feedback.

items.stem: Explain how hormones control the menstrual cycle and how this knowledge is used in IVF.
items.answer: FSH, LH, oestradiol, progesterone; follicular phase, ovulation, luteal phase; negative and positive feedback; corpus luteum; menstruation; IVF: down-regulation, FSH superovulation, hCG trigger, egg collection, fertilisation, embryo transfer, progesterone support.
items.markingKey: FSH, LH, oestradiol, progesterone; follicular phase, ovulation, luteal phase; negative and positive feedback; corpus luteum; menstruation; IVF: down-regulation, FSH superovulation, hCG trigger, egg collection, fertilisation, embryo transfer, progesterone support.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)"?
options: Three or more alleles of a gene in a population, such as Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i for ABO blood groups
Inheritance of a characteristic controlled by many genes, each with a small additive effect
A cross involving two genes, each with two alleles
A hormone from the anterior pituitary that stimulates development of follicles in the ovary and secretion of oestradiol
items.answer: A hormone from the anterior pituitary that stimulates development of follicles in the ovary and secretion of oestradiol
items.markingKey: D. "follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)" is a hormone from the anterior pituitary that stimulates development of follicles in the ovary and secretion of oestradiol.

items.stem: Explain the roles of hormones in the menstrual cycle.
items.answer: FSH from the pituitary stimulates follicle development and oestradiol secretion; oestradiol thickens the endometrium and at high levels causes positive feedback giving an LH surge; LH triggers ovulation and formation of the corpus luteum; progesterone maintains the endometrium and inhibits FSH/LH; corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, menstruation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: FSH from the pituitary stimulates follicle development and oestradiol secretion; oestradiol thickens the endometrium and at high levels causes positive feedback giving an LH surge; LH triggers ovulation and formation of the corpus luteum; progesterone maintains the endometrium and inhibits FSH/LH; corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, menstruation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Plasma progesterone fell from 13.4 ng cm⁻³ on day 22 to 3.1 ng cm⁻³ on day 28. Calculate the percentage change and suggest a biological explanation for it.
items.answer: -76.9 %; the corpus luteum degenerates when no hCG is produced, so progesterone falls and menstruation begins.
items.markingKey: % change = (3.1 − 13.4)/13.4 × 100 (M1) = -76.9 % (A1). Explanation (R1): the corpus luteum degenerates when no hCG is produced, so progesterone falls and menstruation begins.

items.stem: "IVF should be freely available to all who want it." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: IVF should be available on the basis of medical need and likelihood of success, with limits to manage costs and risks.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: allows infertile couples to have children; success rates improving. Arguments against: high cost to health systems; low success rates in older women; risk of multiple births and ovarian hyperstimulation; ethical issues about spare embryos. Supported judgement: IVF should be available on the basis of medical need and likelihood of success, with limits to manage costs and risks. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "pollination"?
options: The structure formed from the follicle after ovulation, which secretes progesterone
Variation in which individuals fall into distinct categories, such as blood groups
The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma
Inheritance of a characteristic controlled by many genes, each with a small additive effect
items.answer: The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma
items.markingKey: C. "pollination" is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma.

items.stem: A student claims: "Fruits develop from ovules." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Fruits develop from the ovary wall; seeds develop from ovules.
items.markingKey: Fruits develop from the ovary wall; seeds develop from ovules. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe self-incompatibility in Brassica and explain what it reveals about promotion of cross-pollination.
items.answer: Pollen with an S-allele matching the stigma’s S-alleles is rejected and cannot grow a pollen tube. The genetic mechanism prevents self-fertilisation, maintaining genetic diversity.
items.markingKey: Context (Pollen with an S-allele matching the stigma’s S-alleles is rejected and cannot grow a pollen tube.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The genetic mechanism prevents self-fertilisation, maintaining genetic diversity. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to promotion of cross-pollination.

items.answer: (a) 9.0 µm min⁻¹ (b) 15 % (c) Growth increases up to 15 %, then decreases at higher concentrations.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Declines in insect pollinators are a serious threat to food security."
items.answer: Pollinator decline threatens dietary diversity and some crop yields, though staple calorie supply is less affected; it remains a serious concern.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: about three-quarters of crop types benefit from animal pollination; fruit, nut and vegetable yields depend on pollinators. Arguments against: staple cereals (wheat, rice, maize) are wind-pollinated; managed bees and hand pollination can partly compensate. Supported judgement: Pollinator decline threatens dietary diversity and some crop yields, though staple calorie supply is less affected; it remains a serious concern.

items.stem: Explain how a seed germinates.
items.answer: Water is absorbed (imbibition), activating gibberellin production; gibberellin stimulates amylase production in the aleurone layer; starch is hydrolysed to maltose and glucose for respiration; the radicle emerges, then the plumule; growth by mitosis.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Water is absorbed (imbibition), activating gibberellin production; gibberellin stimulates amylase production in the aleurone layer; starch is hydrolysed to maltose and glucose for respiration; the radicle emerges, then the plumule; growth by mitosis. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Removing the anthers from a flower before it opens prevents:
items.answer: self-pollination
items.markingKey: B. Used in plant breeding.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "allele".
items.answer: One of the alternative forms of a gene, found at the same locus
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: one of the alternative forms of a gene, found at the same locus. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the pattern of inheritance of red–green colour blindness.
items.answer: The gene is on the X chromosome (no locus on Y); the allele for colour blindness is recessive; males (XY) with one recessive allele are affected; females need two copies, so are usually carriers; affected males inherit the allele from their mothers; affected fathers pass it to all daughters.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The gene is on the X chromosome (no locus on Y); the allele for colour blindness is recessive; males (XY) with one recessive allele are affected; females need two copies, so are usually carriers; affected males inherit the allele from their mothers; affected fathers pass it to all daughters. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between dominant alleles and recessive alleles.
items.answer: A dominant allele is expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygote; a recessive allele is expressed only when homozygous.
items.markingKey: A dominant allele is expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygote; a recessive allele is expressed only when homozygous. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: Females can be affected if homozygous recessive, though this is rarer.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Mendel’s laws explain the inheritance of all characteristics."
items.answer: Mendel’s principles underlie inheritance, but many traits need extensions such as codominance, linkage and polygenic inheritance.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: monohybrid ratios for many single-gene traits match Mendel’s predictions. Arguments against: codominance, multiple alleles, sex linkage, linkage and polygenic traits do not fit simple ratios; environment also affects phenotypes. Supported judgement: Mendel’s principles underlie inheritance, but many traits need extensions such as codominance, linkage and polygenic inheritance. items.answer: allele

items.stem: Why is a test cross used with a homozygous recessive parent?
options: The recessive parent contributes only recessive alleles, so offspring phenotypes reveal the other parent’s alleles.
items.answer: The recessive parent contributes only recessive alleles, so offspring phenotypes reveal the other parent’s alleles.
items.markingKey: C. Reveals genotype.

items.stem: Outline one way in which roan cattle shows codominance.
items.answer: Crossing red and white Shorthorn cattle produces roan calves with both red and white hairs. Both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, so both pigments appear.
items.markingKey: Context (Crossing red and white Shorthorn cattle produces roan calves with both red and white hairs.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "linked genes"?
options: A genetic mechanism that prevents pollen from fertilising ovules of the same plant, promoting cross-fertilisation
Genes located close together on the same chromosome, which tend to be inherited together
The spreading of seeds away from the parent plant, reducing competition and colonising new areas
The development of a seed into a seedling, requiring water, oxygen and a suitable temperature
items.answer: Genes located close together on the same chromosome, which tend to be inherited together
items.markingKey: B. "linked genes" is genes located close together on the same chromosome, which tend to be inherited together.

items.stem: Why does crossing over produce recombinants only in a small proportion of gametes for closely linked genes?
options: Crossing over never occurs near genes.
A chiasma is less likely to form in the short region between them.
items.answer: A chiasma is less likely to form in the short region between them.
items.markingKey: D. Distance.

items.stem: Explain the difference between unlinked genes and linked genes.
items.answer: Unlinked genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently, giving 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 in a test cross; linked genes are on the same chromosome, so parental types predominate and recombinants are fewer than 50 %.
items.markingKey: Unlinked genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently, giving 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 in a test cross; linked genes are on the same chromosome, so parental types predominate and recombinants are fewer than 50 %. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In Drosophila, a female heterozygous for body colour and wing length (GgNn, with G and N on the same chromosome) was test-crossed with a ggnn male. Offspring: 284 grey normal, 256 black vestigial, 30 grey vestigial and 26 black normal. Calculate the recombination frequency.
Using Mendel’s dihybrid crosses with peas as an example, explain independent assortment.
items.answer: Crossing round yellow with wrinkled green peas gave F2 of 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow and 32 wrinkled green. The ratio close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 showed that the two genes assort independently.
items.markingKey: Context (Crossing round yellow with wrinkled green peas gave F2 of 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow and 32 wrinkled green.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The ratio close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 showed that the two genes assort independently. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to independent assortment.

items.stem: In maize, a cross between two double heterozygotes produced: 296 purple smooth, 101 purple shrunken, 92 yellow smooth, 31 yellow shrunken. Calculate χ² for the expected 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio and state a conclusion (critical value 7.81, 3 df, p = 0.05).
items.answer: χ² = 0.55; not significant – results fit the expected ratio; accept H₀
items.markingKey: Expected: 292.5, 97.5, 97.5, 32.5 (M1); Σ(O − E)²/E (M1) = 0.55 (A1); comparison with 7.81 and conclusion (A1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The chi-squared test can show whether two genes are linked."
items.answer: Chi-squared can provide evidence for linkage when combined with the pattern of an excess of parental types, but other explanations must be considered.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: a significant deviation from 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 or 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 suggests linkage; excess of parental types indicates linkage. Arguments against: other causes such as reduced viability of some genotypes can also cause deviations; small samples have low power. Supported judgement: Chi-squared can provide evidence for linkage when combined with the pattern of an excess of parental types, but other explanations must be considered.

items.stem: Explain how independent assortment and crossing over lead to new combinations of alleles.
items.answer: Random orientation of bivalents at metaphase I; 2ⁿ combinations; crossing over at chiasmata between non-sister chromatids; exchange of alleles of linked genes; recombinants; contribution to variation.
items.markingKey: Random orientation of bivalents at metaphase I; 2ⁿ combinations; crossing over at chiasmata between non-sister chromatids; exchange of alleles of linked genes; recombinants; contribution to variation.

items.stem: Why do linked genes not give a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio?
options: They are on the same chromosome and do not assort independently, so parental combinations are more common.
items.answer: They are on the same chromosome and do not assort independently, so parental combinations are more common.
items.markingKey: A. Linkage.

items.stem: Freya writes: "Linked genes are always inherited together." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Crossing over can separate them, producing recombinants.
items.markingKey: Crossing over can separate them, producing recombinants. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A chi-squared value of 2.4 was calculated with 3 degrees of freedom (critical value 7.81). What is concluded?

items.stem: Approximately what percentage of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean in a normal distribution?
Mateo writes: "Continuous variation is caused only by the environment." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is usually caused by many genes as well as environmental factors.
items.markingKey: It is usually caused by many genes as well as environmental factors. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why skin colour in humans shows continuous variation.
items.answer: Skin colour is controlled by many genes affecting melanin production, each allele adding a small amount; environment (UV exposure, tanning) also modifies colour; the combination produces a continuous range.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Skin colour is controlled by many genes affecting melanin production, each allele adding a small amount; environment (UV exposure, tanning) also modifies colour; the combination produces a continuous range. items.answer: 156 and 184 cm
items.markingKey: C. ± 2 SD.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Human height is determined mainly by genes."
items.answer: Genes explain most variation within well-nourished populations, but environment, especially nutrition, strongly affects height across populations and generations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: heritability estimates of about 80 % in well-nourished populations; hundreds of genetic variants identified. Arguments against: average height has risen with nutrition, showing strong environmental effects; heritability depends on the population and environment. Supported judgement: Genes explain most variation within well-nourished populations, but environment, especially nutrition, strongly affects height across populations and generations.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Variation in which a characteristic shows a range of values with no distinct categories, such as height or mass"?
items.answer: continuous variation
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of continuous variation.

items.stem: Which structure secretes progesterone after ovulation?
items.answer: the corpus luteum

items.stem: Explain the difference between monogenic traits and polygenic traits.
items.answer: Monogenic traits are controlled by one gene, giving distinct phenotypes; polygenic traits are controlled by many genes with additive effects, giving continuous variation.
items.markingKey: Monogenic traits are controlled by one gene, giving distinct phenotypes; polygenic traits are controlled by many genes with additive effects, giving continuous variation. items.answer: Intermediate combinations of alleles are far more likely than extreme combinations.

items.stem: Explain the genetic basis of continuous variation and how it can be analysed statistically.
items.answer: Polygenic inheritance; additive alleles; number of classes 2n + 1; probability of extremes; environmental effects; normal distribution; mean, SD, 68 % and 95 %; examples skin colour, height, wheat colour; comparison with discontinuous variation.
items.markingKey: Polygenic inheritance; additive alleles; number of classes 2n + 1; probability of extremes; environmental effects; normal distribution; mean, SD, 68 % and 95 %; examples skin colour, height, wheat colour; comparison with discontinuous variation.

items.stem: Explain the conditions needed for seed germination and the role of gibberellin.
items.answer: Water (imbibition, enzymes, transport), oxygen (aerobic respiration), temperature (enzyme activity); dormancy; gibberellin; amylase; starch → maltose; radicle and plumule growth.
items.markingKey: Water (imbibition, enzymes, transport), oxygen (aerobic respiration), temperature (enzyme activity); dormancy; gibberellin; amylase; starch → maltose; radicle and plumule growth.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "codominance"?
options: Inheritance of a characteristic controlled by many genes, each with a small additive effect
A hormone from the anterior pituitary that stimulates development of follicles in the ovary and secretion of oestradiol
A statistical test comparing observed and expected frequencies to determine whether differences are significant
A pattern in which both alleles in a heterozygote are fully expressed in the phenotype, as in AB blood group or roan cattle
items.answer: A pattern in which both alleles in a heterozygote are fully expressed in the phenotype, as in AB blood group or roan cattle
items.markingKey: D. "codominance" is a pattern in which both alleles in a heterozygote are fully expressed in the phenotype, as in AB blood group or roan cattle.

items.stem: Define the term "linked genes".
items.answer: Genes located close together on the same chromosome, which tend to be inherited together
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: genes located close together on the same chromosome, which tend to be inherited together. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Where is testosterone produced?
options: in interstitial cells of the testes
items.answer: in interstitial cells of the testes
items.markingKey: C. Leydig cells.

items.stem: A student claims: "A larger standard deviation means a larger mean." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: SD measures spread, not the size of the mean.
items.markingKey: SD measures spread, not the size of the mean. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between wind-pollinated flowers and insect-pollinated flowers.
items.answer: Insect-pollinated flowers have large coloured scented petals, nectar and sticky pollen; wind-pollinated flowers have small dull petals, exposed anthers and feathery stigmas and produce large amounts of light pollen.
items.markingKey: Insect-pollinated flowers have large coloured scented petals, nectar and sticky pollen; wind-pollinated flowers have small dull petals, exposed anthers and feathery stigmas and produce large amounts of light pollen. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between codominance and complete dominance.
items.answer: In codominance both alleles are expressed in a heterozygote (e.g. IᴬIᴮ); in complete dominance only the dominant allele affects the phenotype.
items.markingKey: In codominance both alleles are expressed in a heterozygote (e.g. IᴬIᴮ); in complete dominance only the dominant allele affects the phenotype. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Linked genes are always inherited together." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Crossing over can separate them, producing recombinants.
items.markingKey: Crossing over can separate them, producing recombinants. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between LH and FSH.
items.answer: FSH stimulates follicle growth and oestradiol secretion; LH triggers ovulation and the development of the corpus luteum.
items.markingKey: FSH stimulates follicle growth and oestradiol secretion; LH triggers ovulation and the development of the corpus luteum. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between monogenic traits and polygenic traits.
items.answer: Monogenic traits are controlled by one gene, giving distinct phenotypes; polygenic traits are controlled by many genes with additive effects, giving continuous variation.
items.markingKey: Monogenic traits are controlled by one gene, giving distinct phenotypes; polygenic traits are controlled by many genes with additive effects, giving continuous variation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Of 50 seeds placed after the seed coat was scratched, 44 germinated within 7 days. Calculate the germination percentage.
A carrier woman for haemophilia (XᴴXʰ) and an unaffected man (XᴴY) have a son. What is the probability that he is affected?
items.markingKey: B. Son receives Xʰ with probability 1/2.

items.stem: Using Morgan’s fruit fly experiments as an example, explain gene linkage.
items.answer: Crosses of grey-bodied, normal-winged flies with black-bodied, vestigial-winged flies produced far more parental types than expected for independent assortment. The genes are on the same chromosome, and recombinants arise only by crossing over.
items.markingKey: Context (Crosses of grey-bodied, normal-winged flies with black-bodied, vestigial-winged flies produced far more parental types than expected for independent assortment.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The genes are on the same chromosome, and recombinants arise only by crossing over. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to gene linkage.

items.stem: Which hormone level rises first in the menstrual cycle?
items.answer: FSH
items.markingKey: A. Stimulates follicle.

items.stem: A trait is controlled by 4 unlinked genes, each with one contributing (additive) allele and one non-contributing allele. For a cross between two individuals heterozygous at all 4 genes, calculate (a) the number of phenotype classes and (b) the probability that an offspring has exactly 0 contributing alleles.
Burdock fruits have hooks. How are they dispersed?
items.answer: by attaching to animal fur
items.markingKey: C. Animal dispersal.

items.stem: Using roan cattle as an example, explain codominance.
items.answer: Crossing red and white Shorthorn cattle produces roan calves with both red and white hairs. Both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, so both pigments appear.
items.markingKey: Context (Crossing red and white Shorthorn cattle produces roan calves with both red and white hairs.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, so both pigments appear. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to codominance.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The chi-squared test can show whether two genes are linked."
items.answer: Chi-squared can provide evidence for linkage when combined with the pattern of an excess of parental types, but other explanations must be considered.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: a significant deviation from 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 or 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 suggests linkage; excess of parental types indicates linkage. Arguments against: other causes such as reduced viability of some genotypes can also cause deviations; small samples have low power. Supported judgement: Chi-squared can provide evidence for linkage when combined with the pattern of an excess of parental types, but other explanations must be considered.

items.stem: "IVF should be freely available to all who want it." Discuss.
items.answer: IVF should be available on the basis of medical need and likelihood of success, with limits to manage costs and risks.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: allows infertile couples to have children; success rates improving. Arguments against: high cost to health systems; low success rates in older women; risk of multiple births and ovarian hyperstimulation; ethical issues about spare embryos. Supported judgement: IVF should be available on the basis of medical need and likelihood of success, with limits to manage costs and risks. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: "Human height is determined mainly by genes." Discuss.
items.answer: Genes explain most variation within well-nourished populations, but environment, especially nutrition, strongly affects height across populations and generations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: heritability estimates of about 80 % in well-nourished populations; hundreds of genetic variants identified. Arguments against: average height has risen with nutrition, showing strong environmental effects; heritability depends on the population and environment. Supported judgement: Genes explain most variation within well-nourished populations, but environment, especially nutrition, strongly affects height across populations and generations. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. items.stem: Describe the structure of an insect-pollinated flower and explain the processes of pollination, fertilisation and seed dispersal.
items.answer: Sepals, petals, stamens (anther, filament), carpel (stigma, style, ovary, ovule); adaptations for insects; cross-pollination and self-incompatibility; pollen tube growth; double fertilisation; seed and fruit formation; dispersal by wind, animals, explosive mechanisms; germination.
items.markingKey: Sepals, petals, stamens (anther, filament), carpel (stigma, style, ovary, ovule); adaptations for insects; cross-pollination and self-incompatibility; pollen tube growth; double fertilisation; seed and fruit formation; dispersal by wind, animals, explosive mechanisms; germination.
